direction.comments: The direction on a macroscale blends multiple styles of movies into one: it plays like a serious drama while satirizing the obsessed artist trope to show how absurd the concept is, its musical and comedy elements are also well directed, and it builds its world by mixing the feel of an obsessed artist movie with Mulholland Drive-esque dream sequences and Wes Anderson-style shots that play up the humor and highlight the absurdity of what's going on, all blending together into a very funny and entertaining movie; the direction on a microscale is great, as it's where the comedy comes out and where you see the emotions of these characters and why they do what they do, especially in the interactions between Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, who both give incredible performances that bring out the comedy and sincerity of these moments and show how profound they are to their characters; the storytelling is great, as it's so entertaining for how absurd it is, taking the silly premise of a middle-aged mom joining community theater and painting it as a serious obsessed artist movie, which makes it so funny to watch how far down the rabbit hole Mona goes to be the best actress she could possibly be; the tension is built in a very humorous way, as despite the absurd premise, you really do care about the two leads, so you can't help but cringe when things go wrong

performance.comments: Incredible, showing her character's transformation from a shy, shut-in, middle-aged housewife into someone completely lost in the role and going full method, as breaking out of her shell reveals who she actually is and wants to be, along with the confidence she gains from it; her singing, comedy, and emotions are all good, as she plays a wide range of emotions effortlessly, especially in one monologue around the 30- to 40-minute mark that shows how broken she gets from this role, and her chemistry with Paul Giamatti really makes this movie; she's one of the best actresses of all time and deserves the Oscar for this phenomenal performance

Shows why he's one of the best working character actors right now, playing this role like only Paul Giamatti could, with comedy, vigor, and ferocity, while also showing the emotional side of why he believes in Mona and the theater and why it means so much to him; he shifts octaves and levels to amplify his character's anger and compassion, and his wide range of emotions works so well with Julianne Moore, as their chemistry really makes this movie and brings to life the dynamic of the teacher pushing the obsessed artist

Good in a smaller role, supporting the leads well, and while you don't really understand why her character does what she does, it adds to the interpretation that Mona sees everything through rose-colored glasses, so not all of it may be real because of how naive she is about this community theater program
Barely in the movie, but it's nice to see him in a movie he directed

cast.comments: Works well in supporting Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, whose chemistry is what really makes this movie

story.comments: The concept is what makes this movie so much fun, as it's a satire of the obsessed artist trope about a middle-aged housewife who joins a community theater production led by a very rigid and strict director and gets lost in such a small part, coming out of her shell to reveal what has been hiding inside her the entire time, and following her down that rabbit hole is what makes it so funny; the plot structure is linear, following her from joining the production all the way to the actual performance, and I wouldn't cut anything out; character writing is great, which is essential for an obsessed artist movie since it has to show what the characters are thinking and why they become so obsessed: Mona starts as a shy character who can't open up until one scene where Paul Giamatti's character rips her apart, which unlocks something in her and sends her down the rabbit hole of being the best she can be, because for the first time in her life she has confidence in herself and wants to be taken seriously (perfectly captured when she tells the costume designer, 'I'm not going for glamour, I'm going for reality'), while Paul Giamatti's character shows why he does community theater and why he pushes and supports Mona because of his own career and how he sees himself, bringing the classic dynamic of a teacher pushing the obsessed artist to life in a humorous way as they push each other to become the best versions of themselves

screenplay.comments: The dialogue is so funny because of how serious it is for such an absurd movie, making it a very well-written satire full of profound lines, like when the director opens up about why he believes in Mona; the humor is a big element of the movie, as the satire of the obsessed artist trope is so funny mainly because of how absurd the premise is, with a middle-aged mom getting lost in community theater and a community theater director pushing his actors like it's Whiplash; the symbolism is very strong, satirizing how far we'll go to be the best by showing that even a middle-aged mom can get lost in a role trying to become the best actor she can be, since it's the first time she has ever believed in herself, while the director pushes his actors for his own particular purpose, making the movie's messaging very profound; the foreshadowing is pretty good and well written, even if it isn't what makes the movie

score.comments: Makes it feel like a comedy musical, as it's written like one and helps add to that tone

soundtrack.comments: Very funny musical numbers, all original songs written by Jesse Eisenberg that are written very well, adding to the comedy and helping bring the community theater musical Nosy Neighbors to life

cinematography.comments: Phenomenal for how it mixes so many different styles, from close following shots that show how raw and invested the performances are, to Wes Anderson-style pans and zooms that show the absurdity of the movie, to dreamy, late-night sequences shot like Mulholland Drive and neo-noir movies that show how lost she is in this dream world, all of which add to the comedy by having the movie take itself so seriously for such a stupid premise

editing.comments: Very well edited, working in conjunction with the cinematography to switch between these different styles of shots, from the dreamy noir-esque sequences to the raw theater play to the comedy, which shows how strong the editing is, even if it's not as strong as the cinematography

sound.comments: Its sound adds to the community theater setting, while also amplifying the tension in some of the obsessed artist moments

production_design.comments: Very much feels like they're rehearsing in a real New Jersey community theater, and it's designed so well, including the moving and workshopped sets of the play that help make this movie

makeup.comments: The hairstyling and makeup are good, showing how deep she gets into the role and adding to the comedy

costumes.comments: Very much the costumes you would see in a community theater play, and they're also a key plot point, as she wants a realistic interpretation of her character rather than a glamorous version

review.pacing: Paced perfectly, as you really could not add or cut anything
review.climax: So good, as the play itself shows how deep she is in character and how much it affects her life, even when people try to get her to break character
review.tone: A satire of the obsessed artist movie, similar to Theater Camp in how it pokes fun at theater, mixing the raw grittiness of obsession with absurd Wes Anderson-style zooms and pans and dreamy David Lynch-esque noir sequences, all of which show how absurd this movie is
review.final_notes: Saw it as the opening night film at Austin Film Festival, and it's the best film of the festival
review.overall: Overall, 'The Debut' redefines the obsessed artist subgenre by satirizing it into something so absurd (a middle-aged mom getting lost in her role in community theater) that it's just so funny, while also being surprisingly profound in showing why its protagonist does what she does; it's all carried by incredible performances from Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, whose artist-teacher relationship is integral to driving this satirical take on the obsessed artist movie into what it is: one of the best movies of the year
